opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about Fawkes is that it flips the usual dynamic. Normally, when people talk about adversarial machine learning, the attacker is the bad guy and the model is the thing being protected. With Fawkes, we asked: what if the individual, the person whose face is being scraped off the internet, could use those same techniques to protect themselves?

The core idea is something we call "cloaking." Before you post a photo of yourself online, you run it through Fawkes, and it makes very small, pixel-level changes to the image. To a human eye, the photo looks basically the same; you look like you. But in the feature space that a deep learning model uses to represent faces, those changes are significant. We're nudging your image's features toward a different identity, someone or something that isn't you.

The key insight is that we're not trying to fool a model at test time the way a classic evasion attack would. We're targeting the training process. Companies like Clearview scrape billions of images from social media and build a model of what you look like. If the photos they collect of you are cloaked, then the model they build of "you" is actually centered on this shifted, distorted representation. Later, when someone takes a normal, uncloaked photo of you, say from a security camera or on the street, and runs it through their system, it doesn't match, because the model learned the wrong thing about your face.

So in a sense it's a form of data poisoning, but targeted and personal. You're poisoning only your own representation, not the model as a whole, which makes it much harder for the tracker to notice something is off.

Of course, it's not a silver bullet. There's an arms race aspect. If they already have lots of clean photos of you, cloaking new ones helps less. And model developers can try to adapt, through robust training or detecting cloaked images. We've spent a lot of time thinking about those countermeasures. But the bigger point for me is that it gives individuals some agency. For years the assumption has been that if your photos are public, you've basically lost control. Fawkes is an attempt to say: no, there are technical tools that can shift that balance of power back, at least a little, toward the people being tracked.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss transferability across facial-recognition models or using one model to approximate another's face representations.

r002.rationale: It says Fawkes makes small pixel-level changes that look essentially unchanged to people but shift the face toward a different identity in a model's feature space.

r003.rationale: It explains that training on cloaked photos makes the model built of the subject learn a shifted representation associated with that subject, describing it as a different identity and the wrong thing about the subject's face.

r004.rationale: It says a later normal, uncloaked photo of the subject will not match the model's learned representation.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that Fawkes isn't really about hiding your face from a camera, it's about poisoning the model that's trying to learn your face in the first place.

The threat we were worried about is something like Clearview AI, where someone scrapes billions of photos off the public web, labels them by identity, and trains a recognizer that can take a photo of you on the street and say, "that's Ben, here's his profile." The key observation is that these models don't actually see you. They see a feature vector, a point in some high-dimensional embedding space, and they've learned that all the photos labeled "Ben" cluster around a certain region of that space.

What Fawkes does is take your photos before you post them, and add very small perturbations, pixel-level changes that are basically invisible to a human looking at the picture, but that push the image's feature representation toward some other person's region in that space. We call it a "cloak." So to you, your friends, your family, it still looks exactly like you. But when the recognizer ingests it as training data, it's learning that "Ben" lives somewhere over here in feature space, next to some random target identity, rather than where you actually are.

And then the nice part is what happens at inference time. Somebody takes an uncloaked photo of you, a real one, maybe from a surveillance camera, and feeds it in. Your actual features land in the real "you" region of the space, but the model has never associated that region with your name. It's been taught that you're somewhere else. So it either misidentifies you or just doesn't match at all.

A couple of things I'd emphasize about why we designed it that way. One is that it has to be a data poisoning approach rather than an evasion approach, because you don't control the photos that get taken of you later. You only control what you put out there. So the protection has to live in the training data, not in the test image. The second is that it needs to be robust, meaning it shouldn't matter too much which specific model architecture the attacker uses. We generate the cloaks against a feature extractor we have, and the hope, which largely held up in our experiments, is that the perturbations transfer across different extractors because those models are learning broadly similar representations of faces.

The honest caveat is that it's an arms race. If the attacker already has a bunch of clean photos of you from before you started cloaking, the protection is weaker, and if the model trainers specifically adapt to this kind of defense, we'd have to adapt too. But the whole point was to shift some agency back to individuals, to give regular people a tool where the default act of sharing a photo doesn't automatically feed a surveillance system.

r001.rationale: It says cloaks are generated against one feature extractor and transfer across different extractors because they learn similar face representations.

r002.rationale: It explains that small, human-invisible pixel changes shift the image's representation toward another person's region.

r003.rationale: It says training teaches the model that the subject's name belongs to a region near a random target identity.

r004.rationale: It explains that an uncloaked photo may be misidentified or fail to match because the model was not taught to associate the subject's real feature region with their name.

astra-6.text:
The way to think about Fawkes is that it gives people a way to influence what a facial recognition model learns about them. Before you put a photo online, you make very small changes to its pixels. To a human, it still looks like you. But to a model, those changes can shift the features it associates with your identity.

If someone scrapes those photos and uses them to train a facial recognition system, the idea is to get that system to learn the wrong representation of you. Then, when it encounters a clean image of you—one you haven’t modified—it’s less likely to make the connection.

So the protection is really about disrupting the learning process. It isn’t making your face invisible, and it isn’t a guarantee against a system that already knows what you look like. It’s a way to push back on the use of your publicly shared photos as training data.

r001.rationale: The response does not explain transferability or using one model to approximate how other models represent a face.

r002.rationale: It says tiny pixel changes leave the photo looking like the subject to a human while shifting the features a model associates with their identity and causing it to learn a wrong representation.

r003.rationale: It does not say the model associates the subject’s name with another person’s facial features.

r004.rationale: It explains that after training on modified photos, a system is less likely to connect a clean, unmodified image to the subject.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about Fawkes is that it gives people a way to push back on facial recognition systems that learn from their photos without their consent. Before you put a photo online, you make very small changes to it—changes that are hard for a human to see, but that affect how a machine-learning model interprets your face.

The goal isn’t simply to stop a system from detecting a face in that particular picture. It’s to interfere with what the system learns about you. If someone scrapes those modified photos to train a recognition model, they learn the wrong representation of your face. Then, when they encounter a real, unmodified photo of you, that representation doesn’t match.

So it’s a form of data poisoning, but used defensively. And the distinction matters: it’s about protecting against future training on your photos, rather than erasing what an existing system may already know about you.

r001.rationale: The response does not describe transferability across models or using one model to approximate another.

r002.rationale: It says the changes are hard for humans to see and affect a model’s interpretation, but does not explain that the model represents the face as a different person.

r003.rationale: It describes a wrong representation, but does not say the model associates the subject’s name with another person’s facial features.

r004.rationale: It says that after training on modified photos, the representation will not match when the model encounters a real, unmodified photo, communicating a subsequent identification failure.
